abstract_excerpt: This paper describes the rise of task primitives in robot learning from observation. A framework is developed that uses observed data to initially learn a task and the agent then goes on to increase its performance through repeated task performance (learning from practice). Data that is collected while the human performs a task is parsed into small parts of the task called primitives. Modules are created for each primitive that encode the movements required during the performance of the primitive, and when and where the primitives are performed. The feasibility of this method is currently being tested with agents that learn to play a virtual and an actual air hockey game.

abstract_excerpt: Visual tracking of unknown objects is an essential task in robotic perception, of importance to a wide range of applications. In the general scenario, the robot has no full 3D model of the object beforehand, just the partial view of the object visible in the first video frame. A tracker with this information only will inevitably lose track of the object after occlusions or large out-of-plane rotations. The way to overcome this is to incrementally learn the appearances of new views of the object. However, this bootstrapping approach is sensitive to drifting due to occasional inclusion of the background into the model.
